name: Hydrogen
everydayExample: Makes balloons float and voices squeaky.
summary: Hydrogen is the first and lightest element, a colorless gas essential for life and a key component of water and organic molecules.

name: Helium
safetyNotes: Inert gas; asphyxiant in high concentrations
everydayExample: The secret giggle in party balloons.
summary: Helium is a very light, unreactive noble gas known for filling balloons and its use in deep-sea diving and cryogenics.

name: Lithium
everydayExample: Powers your phone and keeps things chill.
summary: Lithium is a soft, highly reactive alkali metal, crucial for rechargeable batteries and used in pharmaceuticals and aerospace alloys.

name: Beryllium
everydayExample: The secret ingredient in super-strong, lightweight alloys.
summary: Beryllium is a lightweight but strong alkaline earth metal, used in high-tech applications like aerospace components and X-ray equipment.

name: Boron
everydayExample: Makes your kitchen glassware shatterproof.
summary: Boron is a metalloid with applications ranging from strengthening glass (borosilicate) to being a key component in semiconductors and control rods in nuclear reactors.

name: Carbon
everydayExample: The building block of you, your dog, and your diamond ring.
summary: Carbon is the basis of all known life, capable of forming a vast number of compounds. It exists in various forms, including graphite, diamond, and charcoal.

name: Nitrogen
everydayExample: Makes up most of the air you breathe and keeps your chips fresh.
summary: Nitrogen is a major component of Earth's atmosphere and is essential for all living organisms, primarily in proteins and nucleic acids. It's also used in fertilizers and cryogenics.

name: Oxygen
everydayExample: The reason we can breathe and have campfires.
summary: Oxygen is a highly reactive nonmetal, vital for respiration in most terrestrial life and for combustion processes.

name: Fluorine
everydayExample: Fights cavities in your toothpaste.
summary: Fluorine is the most electronegative and reactive of all elements. It is a pale yellow-green gas, used in toothpaste and refrigerants.

name: Neon
everydayExample: The bright red glow of city nightlife.
summary: Neon is a noble gas that gives a distinct reddish-orange glow when used in vacuum discharge tubes, famously used for advertising signs.

name: Sodium
everydayExample: Half of your table salt and the orange glow in streetlights.
summary: Sodium is a highly reactive alkali metal. It is a vital electrolyte for living organisms and a key component of table salt (sodium chloride).

name: Magnesium
everydayExample: Keeps old Volkswagen Beetles light and makes fireworks bright.
summary: Magnesium is a light, strong alkaline earth metal, important for both biological and industrial processes, from enzyme function to manufacturing lightweight alloys.

name: Aluminium
everydayExample: Wraps your leftovers and builds airplanes.
summary: Aluminium is a lightweight, durable, and corrosion-resistant metal, making it incredibly useful for everything from beverage cans to aircraft construction.

name: Silicon
everydayExample: The brain of your computer.
summary: Silicon is a metalloid that is the principal component of most semiconductor devices, effectively forming the basis of modern electronics.

name: Phosphorus
safetyNotes: White phosphorus is highly toxic and flammable
everydayExample: The 'P' in your DNA and the tip of a matchstick.
summary: Phosphorus is a nonmetal essential for life, forming a key part of DNA, RNA, and ATP. It exists in several forms, some of which are highly reactive.

name: Sulfur
safetyNotes: Can produce toxic gases when burned
everydayExample: Gives rotten eggs their lovely smell.
summary: Sulfur is a bright yellow nonmetal known for its distinctive smell in compounds like hydrogen sulfide. It is essential for life and a key industrial chemical.

name: Chlorine
everydayExample: Keeps your swimming pool clean.
summary: Chlorine is a highly reactive halogen gas, widely used as a disinfectant in water treatment and as a component in many plastics, such as PVC.

name: Argon
everydayExample: Provides the protective atmosphere for welding.
summary: Argon is the third-most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere. As an inert noble gas, it is often used to create a protective atmosphere for welding and in incandescent light bulbs.

name: Potassium
everydayExample: The 'K' in a banana's nutritional facts.
summary: Potassium is a soft, reactive alkali metal that is an essential nutrient for plants and animals, playing a key role as an electrolyte in the body.

name: Calcium
everydayExample: Builds strong bones and makes chalk.
summary: Calcium is an alkaline earth metal vital for living organisms, particularly in cell physiology and as the primary component of bones, teeth, and shells.

name: Scandium
everydayExample: Makes high-performance bicycles super light and strong.
summary: Scandium is a silvery-white transition metal, often used in small quantities to create strong, lightweight alloys for aerospace components and sports equipment.

name: Titanium
everydayExample: Used in jet engines and replacement hips.
summary: Titanium is a transition metal prized for its high strength-to-weight ratio and excellent corrosion resistance, making it crucial in aerospace, medical implants, and pigments.

name: Vanadium
everydayExample: The secret to extra-tough tools and springs.
summary: Vanadium is a hard, silvery-grey transition metal that significantly increases the strength and toughness of steel when used as an alloying agent.

name: Chromium
safetyNotes: Hexavalent chromium is toxic and carcinogenic
everydayExample: The shiny finish on your car's bumper.
summary: Chromium is a hard, shiny transition metal known for its use in stainless steel and chrome plating, which provide corrosion resistance and a decorative finish.

name: Manganese
safetyNotes: Essential nutrient, but toxic in excess
everydayExample: Helps make steel strong and clear glass clear.
summary: Manganese is a brittle, hard transition metal that is a crucial component in steel manufacturing to improve strength and workability.

name: Iron
everydayExample: The backbone of bridges and in your blood.
summary: Iron is a transition metal that is the most common element on Earth by mass, forming much of Earth's outer and inner core. It is the primary component of steel and is essential for life.

name: Cobalt
everydayExample: Gives glass its beautiful deep blue color.
summary: Cobalt is a hard, ferromagnetic transition metal used in high-strength alloys, powerful magnets, and as a distinctive blue pigment in art and glass.

name: Nickel
everydayExample: The 'nickel' in a nickel coin and a key part of stainless steel.
summary: Nickel is a corrosion-resistant transition metal primarily used in the production of stainless steel, coins, and rechargeable batteries.

name: Copper
safetyNotes: Essential nutrient; toxic in high doses
everydayExample: The stuff inside your electrical cords and pennies.
summary: Copper is a ductile transition metal with very high thermal and electrical conductivity, making it essential for electrical wiring, plumbing, and coinage.

name: Zinc
everydayExample: The protective coating on nails and a key ingredient in sunscreen.
summary: Zinc is a metal commonly used as a protective coating for steel (galvanization) to prevent rust. It's also an essential mineral for human health.

name: Gallium
everydayExample: A metal that melts in your hand.
summary: Gallium is a soft, silvery metal with a low melting point, allowing it to melt in the hand. It is critical for modern electronics, including LEDs and semiconductors.

name: Germanium
everydayExample: Used in night-vision goggles and early transistors.
summary: Germanium is a lustrous, hard-brittle metalloid used in early semiconductors and now primarily in fiber optics and infrared optics.

name: Arsenic
everydayExample: A famous poison in old mystery novels.
summary: Arsenic is a notoriously toxic metalloid. While historically used as a poison, it has industrial applications in alloys and semiconductors.

name: Selenium
safetyNotes: Essential nutrient; toxic in high doses
everydayExample: Helps make red glass and can be found in anti-dandruff shampoo.
summary: Selenium is a nonmetal with photovoltaic and photoconductive properties, making it useful in electronics like photocells. It is also an essential micronutrient.

name: Bromine
discoverer: Antoine Jérôme Balard & Carl Jacob Löwig
everydayExample: One of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.
summary: Bromine is a fuming, reddish-brown liquid at room temperature, one of only two elements to be so. It is a reactive halogen used in flame retardants and agricultural chemicals.

name: Krypton
everydayExample: Superman's home planet, but here on Earth, it's used in high-powered lasers.
summary: Krypton is an unreactive noble gas used in certain types of lighting and lasers, and as an insulating gas in high-performance windows.

name: Rubidium
everydayExample: Helps make atomic clocks incredibly accurate.
summary: Rubidium is a soft, silvery-white alkali metal that is highly reactive. It is used in specialized applications like atomic clocks and gives fireworks a purple color.

name: Strontium
everydayExample: Gives fireworks and flares their brilliant red color.
summary: Strontium is an alkaline earth metal known for producing a brilliant crimson flame, making it a key ingredient in red fireworks and flares.

name: Yttrium
everydayExample: Helped create the red color in old CRT television screens.
summary: Yttrium is a silvery-metallic transition metal often found with rare earth elements. It is used in phosphors (like those in old TVs), lasers, and superconductors.

name: Zirconium
everydayExample: Used to make cubic zirconia, the fake diamond.
summary: Zirconium is a strong, corrosion-resistant transition metal used in harsh environments like nuclear reactors and chemical plants. Its oxide is used to create the diamond simulant, cubic zirconia.

name: Niobium
everydayExample: Strengthens steel for jet engines and particle accelerators.
summary: Niobium is a light grey, crystalline, and ductile transition metal. It is primarily used in alloys, especially for creating the high-strength steel used in pipelines and jet engines.

name: Molybdenum
safetyNotes: Essential trace element; toxic in high doses
everydayExample: A key component in high-strength, high-temperature steel alloys.
summary: Molybdenum is a silvery-white transition metal with a very high melting point. It is mainly used in alloys to increase strength, hardness, and resistance to corrosion.

name: Technetium
everydayExample: A radioactive tracer used in medical scans to see inside your body.
summary: Technetium is the lightest element with no stable isotopes. This radioactive transition metal is widely used in nuclear medicine for diagnostic imaging procedures.

name: Ruthenium
everydayExample: Hardens platinum for durable electrical contacts.
summary: Ruthenium is a rare transition metal belonging to the platinum group. It is used as a hardening agent for other metals and as a versatile catalyst in the chemical industry.

name: Rhodium
everydayExample: One of the world's most expensive metals, used to clean car exhaust fumes.
summary: Rhodium is a rare, silvery-white, hard, and corrosion-resistant transition metal. It is one of the most valuable precious metals, primarily used in catalytic converters for vehicles.

name: Palladium
everydayExample: A precious metal used in 'white gold' and car exhaust systems.
summary: Palladium is a rare and lustrous silvery-white transition metal. Like rhodium, its largest use is in catalytic converters, but it is also used in jewelry and electronics.

name: Silver
everydayExample: Used in mirrors, fancy cutlery, and to fight werewolves.
summary: Silver is a precious transition metal known for its brilliant luster and high electrical and thermal conductivity. It has been used for millennia in currency, jewelry, and tableware.

name: Cadmium
discoverer: Friedrich Stromeyer & Karl Samuel Leberecht Hermann
everydayExample: Used to make bright yellow and red paints.
summary: Cadmium is a soft, bluish-white toxic metal. It is used in rechargeable batteries, pigments, and as a corrosion-resistant plating for steel.

name: Indium
everydayExample: The transparent conductor on your smartphone's screen.
summary: Indium is a very soft, silvery-white post-transition metal. Its most notable application is in indium tin oxide (ITO), used to make transparent conductive coatings on touch screens and LCDs.

name: Tin
everydayExample: The coating inside food cans to prevent corrosion.
summary: Tin is a soft, malleable post-transition metal that resists corrosion, making it ideal for plating steel cans. It is also a major component of solder and various alloys like bronze.

name: Antimony
everydayExample: Helps prevent your sofa from catching fire.
summary: Antimony is a brittle, silvery-white metalloid. It is primarily used in flame retardants and to harden lead for use in batteries and ammunition.

name: Tellurium
everydayExample: Gives you 'garlic breath' if you're exposed to it.
summary: Tellurium is a brittle, silvery-white metalloid that is chemically related to selenium and sulfur. It is used in alloys to improve machinability and in some solar panels.

name: Iodine
everydayExample: The antiseptic used to clean cuts and added to table salt.
summary: Iodine is a bluish-black solid halogen that sublimes into a violet gas. It is an essential mineral for thyroid function and is widely used as an antiseptic.

name: Xenon
everydayExample: The bright, blue-white light in high-end car headlights.
summary: Xenon is a dense, unreactive noble gas. It is used in specialized light sources, such as photographic flashes and high-intensity car headlamps, and as a general anesthetic.

name: Caesium
everydayExample: The heart of the atomic clocks that define what a 'second' is.
summary: Caesium is an extremely reactive alkali metal with a low melting point. It is most famous for its use in atomic clocks, which provide the standard for timekeeping.

name: Barium
everydayExample: The chalky 'milkshake' you drink for certain medical X-rays.
summary: Barium is a soft, silvery alkaline earth metal. Its compounds are used in a variety of applications, from providing contrast in medical X-rays to creating green colors in fireworks.

name: Lanthanum
everydayExample: Used in high-quality camera lenses to reduce distortion.
summary: Lanthanum is a soft, ductile, silvery-white metal that is the first element of the lanthanide series. It is used in high-end camera lenses and as a component in lighter flints.

name: Cerium
discoverer: Martin Heinrich Klaproth, Jöns Jacob Berzelius & Wilhelm Hisinger
everydayExample: The spark in your lighter flint comes from cerium.
summary: Cerium is the most abundant of the rare earth elements. It is a key component of the mischmetal used in lighter flints and is also used for polishing glass.

name: Praseodymium
everydayExample: Gives glass a yellow-green color, used in welder's goggles.
summary: Praseodymium is a soft, silvery, malleable and ductile metal, valued for its magnetic, electrical, chemical, and optical properties. It is used to create strong magnets and to color glass yellow.

name: Neodymium
everydayExample: The super-strong magnets in your headphones and electric motors.
summary: Neodymium is a lanthanide whose alloys are used to make the most powerful permanent magnets known, which are essential components in headphones, microphones, and electric motors.

name: Promethium
discoverer: Jacob A. Marinsky, Lawrence E. Glendenin & Charles D. Coryell
everydayExample: Used to make things glow in the dark, like on watch dials.
summary: Promethium is a radioactive lanthanide, with all its isotopes being unstable. It is used in specialized atomic batteries and as a source of beta radiation for luminous paints.

name: Samarium
everydayExample: Used in high-temperature magnets and as a neutron absorber in nuclear reactors.
summary: Samarium is a moderately hard, silvery lanthanide. Its main uses are in samarium-cobalt magnets, which have high-temperature resistance, and as a neutron absorber in nuclear control rods.

name: Europium
everydayExample: Creates the red color in TVs and the glow on euro banknotes under UV light.
summary: Europium is the most reactive of the rare earth elements. It is crucial for producing the red phosphor in television screens and fluorescent lamps and is also used as an anti-counterfeiting measure in euro banknotes.

name: Gadolinium
everydayExample: Helps doctors see your organs more clearly in an MRI scan.
summary: Gadolinium is a silvery-white lanthanide with unusual magnetic properties. It is most commonly used as a contrast agent in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans.

name: Terbium
everydayExample: Provides the green color in smartphone screens and fluorescent lights.
summary: Terbium is a silvery-rare earth metal that is malleable and ductile. It is primarily used to produce the green phosphors found in fluorescent lamps and television screens.

name: Dysprosium
everydayExample: Added to magnets in electric vehicles to help them resist demagnetization.
summary: Dysprosium is a rare earth element used as an additive in neodymium magnets to improve their performance at high temperatures, making it vital for electric vehicle motors.

name: Holmium
everydayExample: Used to create the most powerful artificially generated magnetic fields.
summary: Holmium has the highest magnetic strength of any element, making it useful for creating powerful magnets. It is also used to color cubic zirconia and glass yellow or red.

name: Erbium
everydayExample: Its pink ions are used to amplify signals in fiber optic cables.
summary: Erbium is a lanthanide with important applications in fiber optics, where it is used as a signal amplifier. It also gives glass and ceramics a characteristic pink color.

name: Thulium
everydayExample: Used in portable X-ray devices for medical diagnostics.
summary: Thulium is the least abundant of the stable rare earth elements. When bombarded in a nuclear reactor, it produces an isotope used as a radiation source in portable X-ray devices.

name: Ytterbium
everydayExample: Helps make some of the world's most accurate atomic clocks.
summary: Ytterbium is a soft, malleable, and ductile lanthanide. It has niche uses in portable X-ray sources, as a doping agent for stainless steel, and in ultra-precise atomic clocks.

name: Lutetium
discoverer: Georges Urbain & Carl Auer von Welsbach
everydayExample: Used in detectors for medical PET scans.
summary: Lutetium is the last element in the lanthanide series. It is a very rare and expensive metal with few commercial uses, though some of its isotopes are used in cancer therapy and as detectors in PET scans.

name: Hafnium
everydayExample: Used in the control rods of nuclear submarines.
summary: Hafnium is a lustrous, silvery-gray transition metal chemically similar to zirconium. It is an excellent neutron absorber, making it ideal for use in nuclear control rods.

name: Tantalum
everydayExample: A key component in the tiny capacitors found in smartphones.
summary: Tantalum is a rare, hard, blue-gray transition metal that is highly corrosion-resistant. It is used to make capacitors for electronic equipment and for medical implants due to its biocompatibility.

name: Tungsten
everydayExample: The filament that glows in an old-fashioned incandescent light bulb.
summary: Tungsten has the highest melting point of all elements, making it famous for its use as the filament in incandescent light bulbs. It is also used in superalloys and armor-piercing projectiles.

name: Rhenium
discoverer: Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke & Otto Berg
everydayExample: Added to jet engine turbine blades to withstand extreme temperatures.
summary: Rhenium is one of the rarest elements in Earth's crust and has the third-highest melting point. It is added to high-temperature superalloys used in jet engine components.

name: Osmium
everydayExample: Used to make the ultra-durable tips of high-end fountain pens.
summary: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element. This hard, brittle, blue-gray transition metal is used to create very hard alloys for applications like electrical contacts and fountain pen tips.

name: Iridium
everydayExample: The thin layer of this element found worldwide is evidence of the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs.
summary: Iridium is the second-densest element and the most corrosion-resistant metal known. It is used in high-performance spark plugs and crucibles for growing crystals.

name: Platinum
everydayExample: A precious metal used in fine jewelry and to clean car exhaust.
summary: Platinum is a dense, malleable, ductile, and highly unreactive precious transition metal. It is valued in jewelry and widely used as a catalyst in catalytic converters and scientific equipment.

name: Gold
everydayExample: Makes engagement rings and flashy YouTube thumbnails.
summary: Gold is a bright, slightly reddish-yellow, dense, soft, malleable, and ductile precious metal. It has been a symbol of wealth and used in coinage and jewelry for thousands of years.

name: Mercury
everydayExample: The silvery liquid in old thermometers.
summary: Mercury is the only metallic element that is liquid at standard conditions. This heavy, silvery metal is highly toxic and its use is now limited, but it was historically used in thermometers and barometers.

name: Thallium
everydayExample: A notorious poison, once used in rat poisons.
summary: Thallium is a soft, gray post-transition metal that resembles tin but discolors when exposed to air. It is extremely toxic and was formerly used in rat poisons and insecticides.

name: Lead
everydayExample: Used in car batteries and the heavy apron you wear for X-rays at the dentist.
summary: Lead is a heavy, soft, and malleable post-transition metal. Its density makes it useful for radiation shielding, but its high toxicity has led to its phasing out from many applications like paint and gasoline.

name: Bismuth
everydayExample: The main ingredient in Pepto-Bismol.
summary: Bismuth is a brittle post-transition metal with a silvery-white color and a pinkish tint. It has low toxicity and is famously used in stomach-soothing medicines like Pepto-Bismol.

name: Polonium
everydayExample: Used in brushes to remove dust from camera film.
summary: Polonium is a rare and highly radioactive metalloid. Discovered by Marie Curie, it is a potent alpha particle emitter used in anti-static devices and notoriously as a poison.

name: Astatine
discoverer: Dale R. Corson, Kenneth Ross MacKenzie & Emilio Segrè
everydayExample: The rarest naturally occurring element on Earth.
summary: Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element, a highly radioactive halogen. Its isotopes are studied for potential use in targeted alpha-particle therapy for cancer treatment.

name: Radon
everydayExample: A radioactive gas that can accumulate in basements.
summary: Radon is a radioactive, colorless, odorless, tasteless noble gas. It is a significant and widespread health hazard due to its radioactivity, which can lead to lung cancer.

name: Francium
everydayExample: One of the least stable elements, it exists for only a few minutes at a time.
summary: Francium is the second-rarest naturally occurring element. It is extremely radioactive and unstable, with its most stable isotope having a half-life of only 22 minutes, limiting its study and use.

name: Radium
everydayExample: Historically used to make watch dials glow in the dark, with tragic consequences.
summary: Radium is a highly radioactive alkaline earth metal, discovered by the Curies. It was famously used in self-luminous paints before its health dangers were fully understood.

name: Actinium
everydayExample: A potent source of alpha particles, but extremely rare.
summary: Actinium is a soft, silvery-white radioactive metal that glows faintly blue in the dark. It is the first element of the actinide series and is about 150 times as radioactive as radium.

name: Thorium
everydayExample: Used in the glowing mantles of gas lanterns.
summary: Thorium is a weakly radioactive metallic chemical element. It is being investigated as a potentially safer and more abundant alternative to uranium for nuclear fuel.

name: Protactinium
everydayExample: A rare and expensive element with no practical uses yet.
summary: Protactinium is a dense, silvery-gray actinide metal that is rare, highly radioactive, and toxic. It has no significant applications outside of scientific research.

name: Uranium
everydayExample: The fuel for nuclear power plants and the core of atomic bombs.
summary: Uranium is a very heavy, weakly radioactive metal best known for its use as a fuel in nuclear power plants and as the fissile material in nuclear weapons.

name: Neptunium
everydayExample: The first transuranic element, named after the planet Neptune.
summary: Neptunium is a radioactive actinide metal that is the first transuranic element. It is primarily a byproduct of nuclear reactor operation and has limited uses.

name: Plutonium
everydayExample: Used to power deep space probes like the Voyager spacecraft.
summary: Plutonium is a radioactive actinide metal used as a fuel in some nuclear reactors, as the explosive core in most modern nuclear weapons, and as a power source for deep space missions.

name: Americium
everydayExample: A tiny amount of it is in your household smoke detector.
summary: Americium is a synthetic radioactive element. Its most common isotope, americium-241, is widely used in ionization-type smoke detectors.

name: Curium
everydayExample: Used on Mars rovers to analyze the composition of rocks.
summary: Curium is a hard, dense, silvery radioactive metal named for Marie and Pierre Curie. It is used as an alpha particle source in spectrometers on space probes like the Mars rovers.

name: Berkelium
everydayExample: Named after Berkeley, California, where it was discovered.
summary: Berkelium is a synthetic radioactive element produced in such small quantities that it currently has no use outside of basic scientific research for the synthesis of heavier elements.

name: Californium
commonUses: neutron source for starting nuclear reactors
everydayExample: An extremely powerful neutron emitter used to kick-start nuclear reactors.
summary: Californium is a radioactive actinide and one of the most powerful neutron emitters known. This property makes it useful as a startup source for nuclear reactors and in certain types of cancer treatment.

name: Einsteinium
everydayExample: First discovered in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test.
summary: Einsteinium is a synthetic, highly radioactive element named after Albert Einstein. It was discovered in the fallout of a thermonuclear explosion and is used exclusively for research.

name: Fermium
everydayExample: The heaviest element that can be created by neutron bombardment.
summary: Fermium, named after Enrico Fermi, is a synthetic element that can only be produced in minuscule amounts. It has no applications beyond basic research.

name: Mendelevium
everydayExample: Named after Dmitri Mendeleev, the father of the periodic table.
summary: Mendelevium is a synthetic element named in honor of Dmitri Mendeleev. It was the first element to be synthesized one atom at a time and is used only for scientific research.

name: Nobelium
everydayExample: Named for Alfred Nobel, creator of the Nobel Prize.
summary: Nobelium is a synthetic radioactive element named after Alfred Nobel. Its chemical properties are not fully known and it is only used for research purposes.

name: Lawrencium
everydayExample: The final member of the actinide series.
summary: Lawrencium is a synthetic radioactive element and the last member of the actinide series. It is named after Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, and has no uses outside of research.

name: Rutherfordium
everydayExample: A superheavy element that exists for only seconds.
summary: Rutherfordium is a highly radioactive synthetic element. Its properties are not well-known due to its extreme instability, limiting its application to scientific study.

name: Dubnium
everydayExample: Another synthetic element with a fleeting existence, studied only in labs.
summary: Dubnium is a synthetic superheavy element. It is highly radioactive and has only been created in very small amounts, so it is only used for research.

name: Seaborgium
everydayExample: Named after Glenn T. Seaborg, a pioneer in synthetic element discovery.
summary: Seaborgium is a synthetic radioactive element named in honor of Glenn T. Seaborg. It is too unstable to have any practical applications.

name: Bohrium
everydayExample: Named for Niels Bohr, a foundational figure in quantum mechanics.
summary: Bohrium is a synthetic element named after Niels Bohr. It has only been produced in a few atoms at a time and is used solely for research.

name: Hassium
discoverer: Peter Armbruster & Gottfried Münzenberg et al.
everydayExample: Named after the German state of Hesse, home to the lab that discovered it.
summary: Hassium is a synthetic superheavy element. It is extremely unstable, and its chemical properties are inferred from its position on the periodic table.

name: Meitnerium
discoverer: Peter Armbruster & Gottfried Münzenberg et al.
everydayExample: Named in honor of physicist Lise Meitner, a pioneer in nuclear fission.
summary: Meitnerium, named for physicist Lise Meitner, is a synthetic element with no stable isotopes and no known applications beyond scientific interest.

name: Darmstadtium
everydayExample: Named after the city of Darmstadt, Germany, where it was discovered.
summary: Darmstadtium is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. Only a few atoms have ever been made, and it is used purely for research.

name: Roentgenium
everydayExample: Named for Wilhelm Röntgen, the discoverer of X-rays.
summary: Roentgenium is a synthetic element named after Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays. It is highly unstable and has no practical uses.

name: Copernicium
everydayExample: Named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus.
summary: Copernicium is a synthetic element, named for Nicolaus Copernicus. It is extremely radioactive and decays within milliseconds, limiting it to research.

name: Nihonium
everydayExample: Named 'Nihon', the Japanese name for Japan, where it was discovered.
summary: Nihonium is a synthetic superheavy element, the first to be discovered in an Asian country. It is extremely unstable and used only for research.

name: Flerovium
everydayExample: Named after the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions in Russia.
summary: Flerovium is a superheavy synthetic element. It is expected to have properties similar to lead but is too unstable for its chemistry to be confirmed.

name: Moscovium
discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research & Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
everydayExample: Named for Moscow, the location of the discovery lab.
summary: Moscovium is a synthetic superheavy element. Its properties are unknown and it has no applications due to its extreme instability.

name: Livermorium
discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research & Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
everydayExample: Named after the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California.
summary: Livermorium is a synthetic superheavy element. It is extremely radioactive, decaying in a fraction of a second, and is of interest only to researchers.

name: Tennessine
discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research & Oak Ridge National Laboratory
everydayExample: Named for Tennessee, home of Oak Ridge National Laboratory.
summary: Tennessine is the second-heaviest known element. It is a synthetic halogen, but its properties are largely theoretical due to its extreme instability.

name: Oganesson
discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research & Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
everydayExample: The heaviest element discovered so far, named after physicist Yuri Oganessian.
summary: Oganesson is a synthetic superheavy element and currently the element with the highest atomic number. It is likely a noble gas but is too unstable to confirm its properties.
